title: You never hear sermons about her.
paragraphs: You never hear sermons about her.
Not really.

People preach David.
Joseph.
Esther.
Paul.
But Tamar?
Most people only remember her story because of what was done to her.
And even then… they rush past it.

Because Tamar’s story forces people to look at something uncomfortable:
what happens when evil happens inside the house that was supposed to protect you.

Not in the streets.
Not from strangers.
Not from pagans.
Inside the family.
Inside the king’s house.
And almost nobody defended her.
That silence still exists today.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
The Bible says Tamar was beautiful.
That detail matters because Scripture is showing you how lust often turns people into hunters instead of humans.
In 2 Samuel chapter 13, Amnon—David’s son—became obsessed with his half-sister Tamar. Not love.
Lust disguised as emotional torment.
The kind that convinces people they are victims because they cannot control sinful desire.
“But here’s what most people don’t realize…”
Sin grows in darkness before it destroys in public.

Amnon entertained it.
Fed it.
Protected it.
And eventually, wicked imagination became action.
The Bible says:
“Amnon was so frustrated on account of his sister Tamar that he made himself ill…” — 2 Samuel 13:2
Read that again.
He became sick because he wanted what God forbade.

That is what unchecked sin does.
It corrodes the mind until evil feels justified.
And some people reading this know exactly what that feels like.
Not necessarily sexual sin.
But secret sin.

The fantasy you kept revisiting.
The bitterness you rehearsed.
The hatred you fed.
The compromise you normalized.
God saw it.
You knew.
Then came the manipulation.
Amnon pretended to be sick and asked King David to send Tamar to care for him.
And David did.
That part hurts.
Because sometimes the people who love you unknowingly hand you into the hands of broken people.
Tamar entered the room innocent.
Amnon had already planned the darkness.
Scripture says:
“But when she brought them near him to eat, he took hold of her…” — 2 Samuel 13:11
And Tamar pleaded with him.

She reasoned.
She begged.
She warned him not to commit such evil in Israel.

Notice something important:
the victim in this story had more spiritual clarity than the prince.
Pain does not mean absence of wisdom.
Brokenness does not mean God abandoned you.
Tamar understood righteousness while Amnon was consumed by corruption.
But he would not listen.
Sin rarely listens once it has fully taken the throne.
And then it happened.

The violation.
The humiliation.
The destruction of innocence.
One verse quietly captures the horror:
“Then Amnon hated her exceedingly…” — 2 Samuel 13:15
That is sin.

It promises fulfillment.
Then leaves disgust.
Satan never shows the second half of temptation.

He shows the thrill.
Not the chains.

The appetite.
Not the devastation.

The pleasure.
Not the emptiness afterward.
And suddenly Tamar—the innocent one—was thrown away like trash.
Some people know this pain too well.

Used.
Violated.
Manipulated.
Discarded.
Not always physically.

Sometimes emotionally.
Spiritually.
Mentally.
People took what they wanted from you and abandoned you afterward.
And the worst part?
Others stayed silent.
The Bible says Tamar put ashes on her head and tore her robe.

Public grief.
Public devastation.
She was shattered in plain sight.
And her brother Absalom told her:
“Hold now your peace…” — 2 Samuel 13:20
Silence.
Again.
Nobody defended her immediately.
Nobody brought justice immediately.
Nobody publicly restored her dignity.
Even David became angry… but did almost nothing.
That detail is terrifying because anger without righteousness changes nothing.
Many people are furious about evil until confronting it costs them something.
But Tamar lived with the consequences.
Alone.
Desolate.
Forgotten by many readers of Scripture.
But not forgotten by God.
That matters.
Because some of you feel invisible in your pain.
People moved on from what destroyed you.

They healed faster than you did.
They forgot faster than you could.
But heaven did not ignore it.
God did not miss the tears nobody respected.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit.”
Near.
Not distant.

Not annoyed by your grief.
Not impatient with your healing.
Not disgusted by your scars.
Near.
But here’s where the story becomes even deeper.
Tamar’s account is not only about human evil.
It is also a mirror of humanity’s condition before God.
Because sin violates everything pure.

Sin destroys innocence.
Sin corrupts families.
Sin twists love into selfishness.
Sin leaves devastation everywhere it spreads.
And no human system can fully heal the damage.
That is why Jesus Christ came.
Not merely to inspire people.
Not merely to teach morals.
He came to rescue sinners and restore the broken.
Isaiah 53 says of Christ:
“He was despised and rejected by men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief…”
Jesus understands rejected people.
He understands humiliation.
He understands injustice.
On the cross, the innocent One was stripped, mocked, abused, and crushed under the weight of sin He did not commit.
Why?

So guilty people could receive mercy.
So broken people could receive healing.
So condemned people could become children of God.

That includes the victim.
And it includes the sinner willing to repent.
Because the Gospel is not pretending evil is small.
The Gospel is God crushing sin through the sacrifice of His Son.
Some people reading this carry Tamar’s pain.
Others carry Amnon’s guilt.
Both need Jesus.

One needs healing.
The other needs repentance.
And without Christ, both remain imprisoned.

You can spend years hiding wounds under functioning smiles.
You can spend years defending secret sin while appearing spiritual.
But God sees deeper than appearances.

God saw Tamar.
God saw Amnon.
God sees you.
You knew.
And still, mercy is being offered through Jesus Christ.

Not because you deserve it.
Not because your pain earned salvation.
Not because religious activity cancels sin.
Salvation is by grace through faith in Christ alone.

The tomb is empty.
The cross was enough.
And no darkness in your past is greater than the power of His blood.
That is the hope most people miss when reading Tamar’s story.

Her pain exposes humanity’s evil…
but Christ exposes God’s mercy.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior for those carrying silent devastation.
Someone you know is silently carrying this kind of pain right now. Share this with them before they disappear deeper into isolation.
